findings.label: Apps are per organization and come from three sources: OpenBot's catalogue, the app directory, and servers added by their address.
Each app carries the actions it offers and the bots that may use each one, so the grant is per app action per bot, not per app.
Account mode is a per-app switch with two values: personal (each person's own account) or shared (one account OpenBot holds for everybody in the organization).
Switching to shared is itself an approval change: it gives each bot that uses the app an approval and makes the app ask before every action that changes something.
The account-mode switch is transactional: every account it leaves behind is ended at the app's service first, and nothing changes unless all of them ended.
Connecting returns one of three next steps: consent (the app's own sign-in page address), form (the boxes an app that takes a key asks for), or connected.
Coming back from a sign-in page proves nothing: confirmConnection asks the app whether the account is really connected and records its answer, because a connection can be ended at the app itself.
A key connection is verified by one safe read-only call, on demand and never on page load, because it counts against the person's own limits at the app.
Authorizations are per action in one answer: authorized, waiting for the person's consent, waiting for an administrator, or unknown.
An OAuth client is only needed for a catalogue app whose vendor will not let OpenBot register one itself, and the client secret is kept in the vault and never answered.

ruledOut.reason: there is none; OpenBot re-asks the app through confirmConnection and recheck
